text: Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD.
reflection: Waiting is one of the hardest things we are asked to do. We wait for test results, for answers to prayer, for doors to open, for relationships to heal. And while we wait, our hearts can grow anxious or discouraged. David knew this. He ended Psalm 27 with a word for anyone in a waiting season: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." He says wait twice, at the beginning and the end. It is as if he knows we need to hear it more than once. Between those two commands is a promise. As we wait with courage, God strengthens our hearts. Waiting on the Lord is not passive. It takes courage to keep trusting when nothing seems to be happening. But God meets us in the waiting with strength. This month we will think about patience and waiting on God. Begin with David's double encouragement: wait on the Lord.
question: What are you waiting for right now, and what would it take courage to do while you wait on the Lord?
prayer: Lord, I wait on You. Give me courage while I wait, and strengthen my heart as You have promised. I will wait, I say, on You. Amen.

text: Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.
reflection: It is hard to wait patiently when others seem to get ahead by doing wrong. David addressed this frustration in Psalm 37: "Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way." Fret means to burn, to become heated with worry or resentment. When we see dishonest people succeed, we can start to fret. Why are they prospering while I am struggling? Is it worth doing right? David's answer is to rest in the Lord. Not to stop caring about justice, but to trust that God sees and will act in His time. Wicked plans may succeed for a while, but they do not last. The rest of the psalm promises that evildoers will fade like grass, while those who wait on the Lord will inherit the earth. Fretting drains our energy and steals our peace. Resting restores both. Is something causing you to fret today? Bring it to God. Then rest in Him and wait patiently.
question: What has you fretting today that you could bring to God and rest in Him instead?
prayer: Lord, I will rest in You and wait patiently for You. Take away my fretting, and restore my peace as I trust You with what I cannot control. Amen.

text: I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry.
reflection: David's testimony in Psalm 40 begins with waiting: "I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry." The words waited patiently in Hebrew are literally waiting I waited, a way of emphasizing how long and hard the waiting was. This was not a quick answer. David waited and waited. But then something beautiful happened. God inclined unto him. To incline means to bend down, to lean in close. It is the picture of someone stooping to hear a small child, or a parent bending over a crib. God bent down to listen to David's cry. The waiting was long, but God was not distant. And when the time came, He leaned in close. If you have been waiting a long time, take heart from David's story. God has not stopped listening. He is not too high or too busy to bend down to you. Keep crying out. Keep waiting. He will incline His ear.
question: What cry could you keep bringing to God today, trusting that He leans in to hear?
prayer: Lord, I waited patiently for You, and You inclined unto me and heard my cry. Even when the waiting is long, help me believe You are near and listening. Amen.

text: The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him.
reflection: In the middle of Lamentations, a book of grief over the destruction of Jerusalem, Jeremiah writes words of surprising hope: "The LORD is good unto them that wait for him, to the soul that seeketh him." He was surrounded by ruins. Everything familiar was gone. Yet he declared that God is good to those who wait. This does not mean God is only good when things go our way. It means His goodness is experienced in a special way by those who keep waiting on Him through hard times. Waiting and seeking go together here. Waiting is not sitting idle. It is actively looking to God, seeking Him while we wait for His answer. And the promise is that we will find Him good. Not just His gifts, but Himself. Sometimes we discover God's goodness most deeply in the waiting room. We learn that He is enough even before the answer comes. Wait for Him today. Seek Him while you wait. You will find Him good.
question: How have you found God good while you were waiting for something?
prayer: Lord, You are good to those who wait for You and seek You. As I wait today, let me seek You, and let me find You good. Amen.

text: It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
reflection: Jeremiah continues his thought: "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD." Two things are good: hoping and quietly waiting. Hope looks forward with confidence that God will act. Quiet waiting is the posture of the heart while we hope. It is not frantic, not complaining, not demanding. It is calm trust. This is not easy. When we are in pain or uncertainty, our instinct is to be loud. We want to fix, push, demand, or worry out loud. Quiet waiting takes a different kind of strength. It means resting our case with God and trusting His timing. Quietness is not the same as silence. Jeremiah himself cried out to God throughout this book. Quiet waiting can include honest prayer. But underneath the prayer is a settled heart that knows God will bring salvation in His time. Today, practice quiet waiting. Hope in God, and let your heart be still.
question: Where could you replace frantic demanding with quiet, hopeful waiting today?
prayer: Lord, it is good to hope and quietly wait for Your salvation. Calm my anxious demands, and teach me the quiet trust of one who knows You are good. Amen.

text: For since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him.
reflection: Isaiah prayed with longing for God to come down and act. And in the middle of that prayer, he wrote this: "since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear, neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him." No one has ever seen a God like ours. And no one can imagine what He has prepared for those who wait for Him. Paul later echoed this verse, applying it to the wonders of God's plan revealed in Christ. Waiting can make us feel like we are missing out. Others seem to move ahead while we stand still. But Isaiah reminds us that God is preparing something for those who wait. It is beyond what eyes have seen or ears have heard. Our waiting is not wasted time. It is the time during which God is preparing. If you are in a waiting season, trust that something good is being prepared for you.
question: What might God be preparing for you during this season of waiting?
prayer: Lord, no eye has seen what You have prepared for those who wait for You. Help me trust that my waiting is not wasted, and that You are preparing something good. Amen.

text: For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
reflection: Habakkuk had asked God hard questions. Why was there so much injustice? Why did God seem silent? God answered, but His answer involved waiting: "For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry." God's plans have an appointed time. They are not random or forgotten. They are scheduled in His wisdom. And notice the apparent contradiction: though it tarry, it will not tarry. From our perspective, it may seem slow. But from God's perspective, it is right on time. It will not be one moment late. This is a word for anyone holding on to a promise. God has not forgotten. The vision will speak. It will come true. But it will come at the appointed time, not necessarily our preferred time. Write down what you are trusting God for. Then wait for it. It will surely come.
question: Which promise of God are you holding on to while it seems to tarry?
prayer: Lord, Your vision is for an appointed time. Though it tarry, it will surely come. Help me hold on to Your promises and wait for Your time, which is never late. Amen.

text: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven…
reflection: Ecclesiastes 3 contains a famous poem about time: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to pluck up, a time to weep and a time to laugh. It begins with this verse: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Life moves in seasons. No season lasts forever. Joyful seasons end, and so do painful ones. Planting is followed by harvest. Weeping gives way to laughing. Recognizing this brings both humility and hope. Humility, because we cannot hold on to good seasons forever. Hope, because hard seasons will not last forever either. It also helps us accept where we are. If you are in a season of planting, do not expect harvest yet. If you are in a season of rest, do not feel guilty for not being busy. Each season has its purpose under heaven. Ask God today what season you are in. Then embrace it, trusting Him with its timing.
question: What season are you in right now, and how could you embrace it rather than resist it?
prayer: Lord, to every thing there is a season. Show me what season I am in, help me embrace it, and let me trust You with its timing. Amen.

text: He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end.
reflection: After listing all the seasons of life, Solomon makes this observation: "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time." Not everything is beautiful right now. Some seasons are painful, confusing, or dull. But in His time, God makes them beautiful. Like a tapestry that looks like a tangle of threads from the back, our lives may seem messy up close. But God is weaving something beautiful, and in His time we will see it. Solomon adds that God has set the world, or eternity, in our hearts. We long for meaning beyond the present moment. We sense there is more. Yet we cannot fully see God's work from beginning to end. We see only a piece. That is why trust is needed. We cannot see the whole picture yet. But God can, and He is making it beautiful. If your life feels like a tangle right now, trust the Weaver. In His time, beauty will appear.
question: What tangled part of your life could you trust God to make beautiful in His time?
prayer: Lord, You make everything beautiful in its time. I cannot see Your whole work, but I trust You are weaving something beautiful in my life. Amen.

text: Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
reflection: James turns to the farmer as an example of patience: "Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain." A farmer cannot rush a harvest. He prepares the soil, plants the seed, and then waits. In Israel, the early rain came in autumn, softening the ground for planting. The latter rain came in spring, helping the crops mature before harvest. The farmer depended on both, and he could control neither. He simply waited, working faithfully, trusting the rains would come. James connects this to waiting for the coming of the Lord. But the principle applies to all of life. Some things cannot be hurried. Growth takes time. Character takes time. Answers to prayer often take time. Like the farmer, we do our part and then trust God for what only He can provide. Be patient today. The rain will come in its season.
question: What part is yours to do faithfully today, and what must you wait on God to provide?
prayer: Lord, like the farmer waiting for the rain, help me do my part faithfully and wait patiently for what only You can give. Amen.

text: Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh.
reflection: After describing the patient farmer, James applies it directly: "Be ye also patient; stablish your hearts: for the coming of the Lord draweth nigh." Stablish means to strengthen, to make firm. A heart that is not established is easily shaken. It swings with every piece of news, every disappointment, every delay. An established heart is anchored. It stays steady even when circumstances change. How do we establish our hearts? By grounding them in what is certain. James points to the coming of the Lord. Whatever else happens, Christ will return. That hope is fixed. When we keep it in view, our hearts become steady. The present struggles, however hard, are temporary. The Lord draws near. This truth also puts our waiting in perspective. We are not waiting aimlessly. We are waiting for Someone. And He is coming. Today, ask God to establish your heart. Anchor it in His promises, especially the promise of His return.
question: What changing circumstance could you face with a heart established in the hope of Christ's return?
prayer: Lord, help me be patient and establish my heart, for Your coming draws near. When circumstances shift, keep my heart steady and anchored in You. Amen.

text: Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer…
reflection: In a long list of instructions for Christian living, Paul places three short phrases side by side: "Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer." They fit together like three strands of a rope. Rejoicing in hope looks forward. We rejoice now because of what God has promised for the future. Patient in tribulation endures the present. When trouble comes, we hold steady rather than giving up. Continuing instant in prayer keeps us connected. Instant means constant, persistent, always ready. Prayer is what makes the other two possible. Hope without prayer can fade. Patience without prayer can turn into grim endurance. But prayer keeps both alive. It keeps us talking to the One in whom we hope and from whom we draw strength. If you are in a hard season, take these three phrases as your plan for today. Look ahead with joy. Hold steady in the trouble. And keep praying.
question: How could rejoicing in hope, patience in trouble, and steady prayer shape your day?
prayer: Lord, help me rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, and continue instant in prayer. Let prayer keep my hope and patience alive today. Amen.

text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith…
reflection: Paul contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." The list continues with meekness and temperance in the next verse. Notice that it is fruit, singular. These qualities grow together as one harvest in a life surrendered to God. And notice longsuffering in the middle of the list. Longsuffering means patience, especially patience with people. It is the ability to endure irritation, offence, and delay without losing our temper or giving up on others. This kind of patience is not a personality trait some people are born with. It is fruit, grown by the Spirit. Fruit grows gradually. You cannot force an apple to ripen overnight. In the same way, patience develops over time as we stay connected to God. If you struggle with impatience, do not just try harder. Stay close to God. Ask God's Spirit to ripen this fruit in you.
question: Where do you most need the Spirit to grow patience in you?
prayer: Lord, longsuffering is fruit of Your Spirit, not something I can produce on my own. Keep me close to You today, and grow patience in me. Amen.

text: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
reflection: Solomon offers two pieces of wisdom in one verse: "Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit." Beginnings are exciting. New projects, new relationships, and new ventures all feel full of promise. But the real value is in the end, in finishing well. Many things are started; fewer are completed. And finishing often requires patience. The second half connects patience and humility. The proud in spirit want things done their way and on their schedule. They are quick to push, quick to complain, and slow to listen. The patient in spirit can wait. They trust the process. They do not need to be in control of every timeline. Pride and impatience often go together. So do humility and patience. If you find yourself frustrated with delays today, ask whether pride is part of it. Let humility grow patience in you, and keep going until the end.
question: Is pride making you impatient anywhere, and how could humility help you keep going to the end?
prayer: Lord, the end of a thing is better than its beginning, and the patient in spirit is better than the proud. Humble me, and help me patiently finish well. Amen.

text: He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly.
reflection: Proverbs often contrasts the wise and the foolish. Here it does so through anger: "He that is slow to wrath is of great understanding: but he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly." Being slow to anger is a sign of great understanding. Why? Because understanding sees more of the situation. It considers other perspectives, possible explanations, and long-term consequences. It does not react to the first impression. A hasty spirit, on the other hand, exalts folly. It puts foolishness on display for everyone to see. Quick tempers lead to words we regret, decisions we cannot undo, and relationships damaged in a moment. Being slow to wrath does not mean never feeling anger. It means not being ruled by it. It means pausing before reacting, giving time for understanding to catch up with emotion. A simple practice can help: when you feel anger rising, pause and breathe. Ask God for understanding. Then respond, rather than react.
question: When anger rises today, what could help you pause and seek understanding before you respond?
prayer: Lord, the one who is slow to wrath is of great understanding. When anger rises today, help me pause, see more clearly, and respond with wisdom. Amen.

text: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
reflection: In the ancient world, the greatest heroes were warriors who could capture cities. But Proverbs points to a greater kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Conquering a city takes armies, strategy, and courage. But ruling your own spirit may be harder. Our emotions, impulses, and reactions can be fierce. Mastering them takes daily discipline and God's help. Many powerful people have conquered nations but could not conquer their own tempers. Their lack of self-control undid their achievements. The person who rules their spirit has a strength that lasts. Self-control is part of the fruit of the Spirit. It is not about suppressing every feeling. It is about not letting feelings take the throne. Where do you most need to rule your spirit? Your words, your reactions, your appetites, your thoughts? Ask God for help there today. That victory is greater than taking a city.
question: Where do you most need God's help to rule your own spirit?
prayer: Lord, ruling my own spirit is greater than taking a city. Show me where I most lack self-control, and give me Your strength to rule my spirit there. Amen.

text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath…
reflection: James gives a short formula for healthy communication: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Most of us do the opposite. We are quick to speak, slow to listen, and quick to get angry. We formulate our reply while the other person is still talking. We interrupt. We assume we know what they mean. James calls us to reverse the order. Be swift to hear. Listen carefully, fully, with genuine interest. Be slow to speak. Think before you answer. Be slow to wrath. Do not let anger take over. These three go together. When we truly listen, we often understand more and react less. When we pause before speaking, our words are wiser. And when we are slow to anger, conflicts cool rather than escalate. The next verse explains why: the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God. Our anger rarely accomplishes God's purposes. Practise James's formula in your conversations today. Listen first.
question: In which conversation today could you practise listening first?
prayer: Lord, make me swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to wrath. Help me listen well today before I speak, and fill my conversations with Your peace. Amen.

text: The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance.
reflection: In Peter's day, some people mocked the promise of Christ's return. Where is He? they asked. Everything continues as it always has. Peter answered, "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance." What looks like slowness is actually patience. God is delaying because He is giving people time to turn to Him. He is not willing that any should perish. Every day of waiting is a day of mercy, a day when someone else might come to faith. This changes how we see delay. When God seems slow, we can remember that His patience has a purpose. And it reminds us that God has been patient with us too. How long did He wait for us to turn to Him? If He is patient, we can be patient. And we can use the time He gives to share His love with others.
question: Who could you share God's love with during the time His patience gives?
prayer: Lord, You are not slack concerning Your promise, but patient, not willing that any should perish. Thank You for Your mercy. Help me share Your love with someone today. Amen.

text: But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
reflection: Just before explaining God's patience, Peter offers a perspective on time itself: "But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." God does not experience time the way we do. He is not bound by clocks and calendars. A single day can carry the weight of a thousand years in His purposes. And a thousand years can pass like a single day. This is humbling. We measure time in minutes and hours, and we grow impatient when things take longer than we expect. But God sees all of time at once. He is never rushed and never late. This is also comforting. Our waiting may feel endless, but it is held in the hands of the eternal God. He is not anxious about timing. He knows exactly what He is doing. When you feel impatient today, remember that God's clock is not like ours. Rest in His eternal perspective.
question: Where is impatience rising in you, and how could God's eternal view of time calm it?
prayer: Lord, with You one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. You are never rushed and never late. Let me rest in Your timing today. Amen.

text: For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him.
reflection: God first promised Abraham a son when Abraham was seventy-five. Then the years went by. Ten years. Twenty years. Abraham and Sarah tried to make it happen their own way, with painful results. Twenty-five years after the first promise, when Abraham was one hundred and Sarah was ninety, the verse tells us: "For Sarah conceived, and bare Abraham a son in his old age, at the set time of which God had spoken to him." At the set time. God had a time in mind all along. It was not the time Abraham would have chosen. By then, it seemed impossible. But that was the point. When Isaac was born, there was no doubt that God had done it. Sometimes God waits until a situation is beyond human help so that His glory is unmistakable. If you have been waiting long for a promise, do not give up. God's set time may be closer than you think. And when it comes, you will know it was Him.
question: Is there a promise of God you are tempted to give up on, and what helps you keep waiting?
prayer: Lord, You visited Sarah at the set time You had spoken. Your timing may seem late, but it is never wrong. Help me hold on to Your promises today. Amen.

text: And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.
reflection: Jacob fell in love with Rachel the moment he met her. He agreed to work for her father, Laban, for seven years in order to marry her. Seven years is a long time. Yet the Bible says, "Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her." Love changed how Jacob experienced time. The years flew by because his heart was set on Rachel. Waiting did not feel like a burden. It felt like an investment in something precious. This shows us something about patience. When we love what we are waiting for, waiting becomes easier. It is not just endurance. It is devotion. The same is true in our walk with God. When we love Him, waiting on Him is not drudgery. Time spent waiting for Him becomes time spent with Him. If you are in a long season of waiting, ask God to deepen your love. Love can make years feel like days.
question: How could a deeper love for God change the way you experience waiting?
prayer: Lord, Jacob's love made seven years seem like a few days. Deepen my love for You, so that my waiting becomes devotion rather than frustration. Amen.

text: For this child I prayed; and the LORD hath given me my petition which I asked of him…
reflection: Hannah had longed for a child for years. Her husband's other wife mocked her for being childless. Each year, at the house of the Lord, she wept and could not eat. One year she poured out her soul in prayer so intensely that the priest Eli thought she was drunk. She promised that if God gave her a son, she would give him back to the Lord. God answered. She bore a son and named him Samuel. Later, she brought him to Eli and said, "For this child I prayed; and the LORD hath given me my petition which I asked of him." Hannah's story is one of persistent prayer through years of pain. She did not give up. She brought her grief to God again and again. And when the answer came, she recognized it as His gift. Is there a prayer you have been praying for a long time? Keep bringing it to God. Pour out your soul to Him, as Hannah did.
question: What long-held prayer could you bring to God again today?
prayer: Lord, Hannah prayed through years of grief, and You heard her. I bring You my long-held prayers again today, trusting that You hear and care. Amen.

text: My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.
reflection: In ancient cities, watchmen stood on the walls through the night, guarding against enemies. The hours were long, dark, and lonely. More than anything, they longed for morning, when their watch would end. The psalmist uses that image to describe his longing for God: "My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning." He repeats the phrase for emphasis. This is intense waiting. Not casual, not distracted, but eager and focused. And notice what he waits for. Not just an answer or a change in circumstances, but the Lord Himself. The watchman knows morning will come. It always does. The psalmist has the same confidence about God. He will come. This psalm begins out of the depths, from a place of deep distress. But it ends in hope. If you are in a long night today, wait for the Lord like a watchman waits for dawn. Morning is coming.
question: If you are in a dark season, how could you watch for God like a watchman waits for morning?
prayer: Lord, my soul waits for You more than they that watch for the morning. In my dark season, give me eager hope that Your coming is as sure as the dawn. Amen.

text: Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me.
reflection: Micah looked around and saw corruption everywhere. Leaders took bribes. Friends could not be trusted. Even family members turned against each other. It would have been easy to despair. But Micah made a decision: "Therefore I will look unto the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation: my God will hear me." Three firm statements. I will look. I will wait. My God will hear. When people disappoint us and the world seems broken, we can choose where to look. Micah did not look to human solutions or wallow in what was wrong. He turned his eyes to God. And he waited with confidence, because he knew God would hear him. Notice the word therefore. Because everything around him was unreliable, he looked to the One who is reliable. Sometimes disappointment with people drives us to God. That is not a bad thing. If people have let you down, look to the Lord today. Wait for Him. He will hear you.
question: Who has disappointed you, and how could you turn your eyes to the Lord instead?
prayer: Lord, when people disappoint me, I will look unto You. I will wait for the God of my salvation, for You will hear me. Amen.

text: And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you: for the LORD is a God of judgment: blessed are all they that wait for him.
reflection: We usually think of ourselves as the ones who wait for God. But Isaiah reveals something surprising: God waits for us. "And therefore will the LORD wait, that he may be gracious unto you, and therefore will he be exalted, that he may have mercy upon you." God's people had trusted in other nations. Yet God did not give up on them. He waited, longing to be gracious. He wanted to show mercy. He was ready the moment they turned back to Him. This is a tender picture of God's heart. Like a parent waiting up for a child, God waits for us to come to Him. He is not reluctant. He is eager to be gracious. And the verse ends with a blessing for us: "blessed are all they that wait for him." So we wait for God, and He waits for us. When we meet, grace flows. If you have been running from God or trusting other things, turn back today. He has been waiting to be gracious to you.
question: Is there something you have been holding back from God, though He waits to be gracious to you?
prayer: Lord, You wait so that You may be gracious to me and have mercy on me. I turn to You today, thankful that You are eager to bless and not reluctant. Amen.

text: And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him.
reflection: Simeon was an old man living in Jerusalem. The Bible describes him as "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him." The consolation of Israel was the promised Messiah, the One who would bring comfort and rescue to God's people. Simeon had been waiting for Him for a long time. God had revealed to him that he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ. Year after year he waited. Then one day, led by the Spirit, he went to the temple and saw Mary and Joseph with the infant Jesus. He took the child in his arms and praised God, saying he could now depart in peace, for his eyes had seen God's salvation. Simeon's waiting was not idle. He was just and devout. He lived faithfully while he waited. And his patience was rewarded. Faithful waiting looks like Simeon. Live rightly, stay close to God, and trust that He will keep His word.
question: What would faithful, active waiting look like for you today?
prayer: Lord, Simeon was just and devout while he waited, and You kept Your word to him. Help me live faithfully as I wait, trusting You to keep Your promises. Amen.

text: And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise.
reflection: Hebrews looks back at Abraham's long journey of faith and sums it up in one line: "And so, after he had patiently endured, he obtained the promise." After he had patiently endured. The promise did not come immediately. Abraham waited decades for Isaac. He never saw the full fulfilment of God's promise to make his descendants as numerous as the stars. Yet he endured. And God kept His word. The writer of Hebrews uses Abraham as an example to encourage believers who were tempted to give up. Their faith was being tested. Some were growing weary. The message was clear: do not quit. God's promises are sure, but they often require patient endurance. There is a phrase in the verse before that is worth noticing too: God swore by Himself, because He could swear by no one greater. His promise is backed by His own character. If you are tempted to give up on a promise today, remember Abraham. Endure patiently. God will keep His word.
question: Where is God calling you to endure patiently as Abraham did?
prayer: Lord, Abraham patiently endured and obtained the promise. Your promises are sure. Give me patience to endure, and keep me from giving up. Amen.

text: For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise.
reflection: The believers who first received the letter to the Hebrews had suffered for their faith. Some had lost property. Others had been publicly mocked. They had endured well at first, but now they were growing weary. The writer encouraged them: "For ye have need of patience, that, after ye have done the will of God, ye might receive the promise." Ye have need of patience. It is not optional. Every believer needs it. There is a gap between doing God's will and receiving His promise. Between planting and harvest. Between obedience and reward. Patience fills that gap. Without it, we may give up just before the promise arrives. Notice the order. First, do the will of God. Then, wait patiently. Then, receive the promise. Many of us want to skip the middle step. But it is there for a reason. It shapes our character and deepens our trust. If you have done what God asked and are still waiting, you are right where you need to be. Be patient. The promise is coming.
question: Have you done what God asked and are still waiting, and how could you be patient in that gap?
prayer: Lord, I have need of patience, that after doing Your will I might receive the promise. Fill the gap between my obedience and Your answer with patient trust. Amen.

text: Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness…
reflection: Paul prayed for the believers in Colosse, and one of his requests was that they would be "Strengthened with all might, according to his glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness." Notice what God's glorious power is for in this prayer. Not for dramatic miracles or impressive displays, but for patience. It takes divine strength to be patient. Our natural strength runs out quickly. We can only wait so long before frustration sets in. But God's power can sustain patience far beyond our natural limits. And Paul adds longsuffering, patience with people, and joyfulness. Not grim endurance, but patience with joy. That is the mark of God's power at work. Anyone can be miserable while waiting. It takes God's strength to wait with joy. Pray this prayer for yourself today. Ask God to strengthen you with all might, according to His glorious power, so that you can be patient, longsuffering, and joyful.
question: Where do you need God's strength to wait with joy instead of frustration today?
prayer: Lord, strengthen me with all might, according to Your glorious power, unto all patience and longsuffering with joyfulness. Help me wait with joy today. Amen.

text: My times are in thy hand: deliver me from the hand of mine enemies, and from them that persecute me.
reflection: David wrote Psalm 31 while surrounded by enemies. People plotted against him, friends avoided him, and he felt forgotten. Yet in the middle of the psalm he made this declaration of trust: "My times are in thy hand." My times. The seasons of my life. The length of my days. The timing of every answer and every deliverance. All of it rests in God's hand. Not in the hands of enemies, not in the hands of chance, and not even in my own hands, but in God's. This is the heart of patient waiting. When we believe our times are in God's hand, we can stop trying to control every outcome. We can trust His timing, even when it does not match ours. This month we have thought about patience and waiting on God. End it with David's simple prayer. Hold up your calendar, your plans, your worries, and your waiting. Then say to God, my times are in Your hand.
question: What season or answer could you entrust into God's hand as this month ends?
prayer: Lord, my times are in Your hand. Every season and every answer rests with You. I entrust my times to You and rest in Your care. Amen.
